transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-05
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~43m
Attendees: Maya, Carlos, Liam (Redwood) — Dr. Arun, Janelle, Sophie, Luke (Northbridge)

Summary (auto): quick review of KV hit-rate delta after eviction retune, conversation about prefix entropy spikes, prompt reuse strategy adjustments. Plan to run extended endurance tests and share security docs.

Topics: benchmark numbers, cache warmup patterns, session affinity, eviction policy, private deployment concerns, next steps.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining; gonna do a quick round robin, call is recorded.
[00:15] Dr. Arun: yep thanks Maya, excited to see the numbers. We had a couple of nights where hit-rate plunged and wanted to see if that's the cache itself or our traffic changes.
[00:30] Carlos: yeah, so quick context — we re-tuned the LRU eviction thresholds last week to favor prefixes that had higher reuse, and we also bumped the prefetch window to 18 tokens for the assistant flows. Initial uplift, but then we saw some entropy spikes.
[00:48] Janelle: to be clear, the entropy we're seeing is per-session? or global? it felt like a small cohort user behavior change.
[01:05] Carlos: good question; the telemetry we captured is mostly per-session shards. We saw a ~6% drop in global KV hit-rate during the 02:00–05:00 UTC window, but if you slice by session id there are thin tails with 20–30% lower reuse — likely several long prompts that defeat prefix reuse.
[01:30] Sophie: those tails correspond to our diagnostic workflows where doctors paste long notes, so that may explain the long prompts.
[01:45] Maya: okay, interesting. So two things: one, we can tune eviction to preserve more long-prefix entries for diagnostic cohort; two, we can evaluate a prompt-normalization preprocessor to canonicalize pasted notes, which might boost prefix hits.
[02:05] Dr. Arun: prompt-normalization worries me slightly about losing clinical nuance — can the preprocessor be conservative?
[02:20] Carlos: absolutely, conservative rules first — strip timestamps, boilerplate headers, repeated whitespace; we avoid semantic compression that could alter meaning.
[02:35] Janelle: we've been experimenting with a light tidy step that removes templates but keeps content, and initial local tests increased reuse for the diagnostic flow by ~12%.
[02:55] Liam: quick note on numbers from our benchmark sheet (link shared in chat): baseline KV hit-rate was 68% before tuning, peaked at 75% after prefetch bump, then intermittent drops to low 62% during the tails. We probably need cohort-aware eviction settings.
[03:20] Maya: thanks Liam — can you drop that sheet into the shared folder? the link is https://redwood.app/sheets/nb-cache-bench (placeholder).
[03:35] Sophie: done, I can see the per-cohort breakdown. There's also memory pressure during the heavy runs, do you recall if that was node-level or cluster-level?
[03:50] Carlos: from logs it's node-level — a few workers hit >85% memory for KV store when many long-prefix entries were retained. We have two levers: increase per-node memory footprint (expensive) or improve eviction heuristics to prefer long-lived keys but still bound memory.
[04:15] Dr. Arun: what's the cost delta if we provision more memory? rough estimate?
[04:25] Liam: provisioning additional dedicated pool nodes would be about a 17–22% cost increase in our model for the pilot window. But if we can recover hit-rate via normalization and cohort eviction, we should keep cost flat.
[04:45] Janelle: question on session affinity — would enabling affinity help reuse? our application tends to route requests arbitrarily today.
[04:58] Carlos: yes, enabling sticky routing (session-affinity) can materially increase reuse because the same KV state stays local. That said, it affects resilience and load balancing. We observed a 9–11% hit-rate gain in a similar customer pilot when using affinity plus a small warmup cache.
[05:20] Maya: re: resilience, we have fallback routing — if node fails we fall back to stateless model variant; but there will be a cold-cache penalty. We can configure a hybrid: soft-affinity where routing prefers a node but can redirect.
[05:40] Luke: from security, sticky sessions raise questions about log separation and PHI handling; we need to ensure KV entries are encrypted and access is auditable. Also, how long do KV entries persist? retention policy?
[06:00] Carlos: retention is configurable per-namespace — default pilot set to 24 hours; encryption in transit is TLS, at rest we integrate with customer KMS for Private deployments. For hosted pilot we can do AES-256 at rest with Redwood-managed keys but for PHI you likely want KMS.
[06:25] Luke: yes we need KMS + audit logs; can you share SOC2 and network diagram?
[06:35] Maya: yes, I'll send SOC2 Type II summary and the network diagram after call.
[06:45] Dr. Arun: back to the numbers — curious if prefix coalescing would help for the diagnostic copy/paste case where there are repeated headers across records.
[06:58] Carlos: prefix coalescing can help: we detect common leading substrings and use canonical ID mapping — it's best when there's stable repeated headers. Downside: risk of false coalescing if headers vary slightly; we can combine with a similarity threshold.
[07:20] Janelle: we already have very similar headers across records; it should help. Will need to test.
[07:30] Maya: action: Carlos will run an experiment combining light normalization + prefix coalescing limited to diagnostic cohort. He'll run the test in a staging job to measure hit-rate and any semantic regressions.
[07:50] Carlos: yep. I'll instrument the run and provide the diff of outputs and hit-rate charts.
[08:05] Liam: quick note about batch sizing — some of your flows are short, smaller batch sizes reduce latency but also reduce batching gains; we recommended adaptive batching which we shipped in the last runtime update.
[08:25] Dr. Arun: can you remind us what adaptive batching does in practice?
[08:33] Carlos: it's workload-aware batching — it favors latency SLOs, enlarges batch windows only when queue length suggests throughput benefits won't hurt latency. For your interactive diagnostic UI we keep small windows.
[08:50] Sophie: on private deployment angle, we're still evaluating network egress and whether we can bring Redwood Private inside our VPC. Any blockers?
[09:05] Maya: technically we support VPC endpoints and on-prem packages; the main blockers are firewall rules and vault/KMS set up. We provided a private deployment checklist last quarter; I'll re-send an updated one.
[09:25] Luke: we'd like an architecture deep-dive for networking next week — I'll coordinate with Maya for availability.
[09:35] Carlos: if we do Private, KV storage can be customer-hosted which solves PHI concerns; plus audit logs live in your cloud. We have patterns for HSM/KMS integration as well.
[09:55] Janelle: small question: when you say KV hit-rate, is that per-token or per-prefix? we saw different numbers in our internal logs.
[10:12] Carlos: good catch — the metrics in the spreadsheet are prefix-level hits. Token-level hit-rate tends to be higher because once a prefix hits the token-level reuse increases through KV cache append. We'll add token-level columns to the sheet.
[10:30] Maya: noted — Liam, please add token-level hit-rate and the cohort slices for diagnostic vs general chat.
[10:40] Liam: will do.
[10:45] Dr. Arun: are there any gotchas we should be aware of with warmup/priming? For example, do warmups cause premature eviction of other keys because of memory churn?
[11:05] Carlos: yes — naive warmup can thrash the cache. We recommend controlled warmup: staggered priming per node and capped warmup windows. Also, using a prioritized insertion where primed keys get lower eviction priority until they’ve been observed in live traffic.
[11:30] Janelle: can Redwood run a simulated warmup based on our sample traces to estimate churn?
[11:40] Carlos: yes that's part of the endurance run we're proposing — we replay sampled traffic to staging with warmup enabled and capture churn and hit-rate deltas.
[11:55] Maya: ok let's talk timeline. We'll do the 48h endurance + light normalization + prefix coalescing test in staging. Carlos will start tomorrow. We'll reconvene in 1 week with results.
[12:12] Dr. Arun: sounds good. One more item: explainability — if cache returns a reused prefix, can we surface provenance so the app knows a response was served from cache?
[12:30] Carlos: yes we add metadata header in the response indicating cache-side hit, prefix id, and last-updated timestamp. That's already in the pilot runtime; we can ensure it surfaces through your SDK.
[12:50] Sophie: that will help our auditors.
[13:00] Luke: one security nit — do those headers contain PII? make sure we don't leak any IDs externally.
[13:15] Carlos: headers contain only internal prefix IDs (hashed) and TTL; no raw PII.
[13:30] Maya: ok moving to wrap-up — recap of next steps and owners, then schedule deep-dives.
[13:40] Liam: recap: 48h endurance, normalization + coalescing test, add token-level metrics, share SOC2 & network diagram, schedule private deploy deep-dive.
[14:00] Dr. Arun: fine. Thanks all.
[14:10] Maya: thanks, we'll follow up in email with timeline and when we kicked off the run.
[14:20] (call ends)

Notes: recorded intermittent crosstalk and a couple of mis-attributed lines (auto-attribution labeled some of Janelle's comments as Speaker 2). Telemetry links and the benchmark sheet were shared in chat rather than pasted into transcript.

References shared: https://redwood.app/sheets/nb-cache-bench (benchmark), https://redwood.app/docs/eviction-policy (eviction doc placeholder), SOC2 & network diagram to be attached by Maya.
